tip: 'Y' replaces location: 'il y habite' = he lives there. It normally sits before the conjugated verb.
'Pour' marks a planned stretch of time, not time already spent: 'pour combien de temps' = for how long you'll be gone. Time already spent usually takes 'pendant'.
'Par' marks the means or channel, like English 'by' or 'via': 'par courriel' = by email. Same in 'par téléphone', 'par la poste'.
Slip a direct object before 'avoir' and the past participle agrees: 'les a lus' grows an 's'. Drop the 'les' and it stays 'lu'.
'Voudrais' is the conditional of 'vouloir'. Used for polite requests.
English says 'wants me to go', but French won't cross two subjects with a plain infinitive: 'veut que j'aille' (subjunctive of 'aller').
'Avoir peur que' (to be afraid that) triggers the subjunctive: 'que ses enfants soient malades'.
Surprise about something already done takes the past subjunctive: 'que personne n'ait remarqué' – 'ait', not the everyday 'a'.
You aren't right in French, you HAVE reason: 'avoir raison'. Being right uses a form of 'avoir' – 'tu aies raison' here.
'Si nous avions' (imperfect past) pairs with the conditional 'nous achèterions'. The 'si' clause itself normally avoids the conditional.
'En' replaces the noun after a quantity word: 'nous en avons acheté deux kilos' = we bought two kilos of it.
'À moins que' (unless) takes the subjunctive: 'à moins qu'il neige' = unless it snows.
English wastes 'water' with no article, but French needs a 'some' word: 'gaspille de l'eau' = wastes some water. Uncountable nouns normally take 'du', 'de la' or 'de l''.
You don't trust someone directly in French – you 'make trust TO' them: 'faire confiance à'. So it's 'lui', not 'le': 'je lui fais confiance'.
When two pronouns stack, 'me'/'te'/'nous' come before 'le'/'la'/'les': 'te le', not 'le te'. 'Je te le promets' = I promise it to you, the reverse of English order.
In a negative command the pronoun stays BEFORE the verb: 'ne lui dis rien'. Only positive commands push it after, as in 'dis-lui'.
'J'en ai entendu parler' = I've heard about it. 'En' replaces 'de' + the topic you heard about.
'Réfléchir à quelque chose' = to think about something. The 'à' phrase collapses to 'y', sitting before the verb: 'il y réfléchit' = he's thinking about it.
'En avoir marre' = to be fed up. The 'en' is baked into the idiom and can't be dropped: 'nous en avons marre' = we've had enough.
'Manquer' flips the subject: 'il me manque' = I miss him, literally 'he is lacking to me'. The person missed is the subject; the one missing them is 'me'/'te'/'lui'.
'Devoir' means both 'must' and 'owe'. Here it's owe, and you owe TO someone: 'nous lui devons beaucoup' = we owe him a lot. So 'lui', not 'le'.
In a positive command the pronoun hooks onto the verb with a hyphen: 'parle-leur' = talk to them. 'Parler à quelqu'un' takes 'leur', not 'les'.
'Répondre à quelqu'un' = to answer someone. French answers TO a person, so the pronoun is 'lui', not 'le': 'tu lui as répondu ?'
'Se souvenir de' (to remember) becomes 's'en souvenir'. Both pronouns go before the verb: 'je ne m'en souviens pas'.
Short adverbs like 'déjà' slip between the two parts of the past tense: 'avons déjà réservé', not 'avons réservé déjà'.
'Dépendre' uses 'de' where English uses 'on': 'je dépends de mes parents' = I depend ON my parents. The preposition often differs from English.
Double pronouns: 'les' (the things given) + 'leur' (to them). 'Les' goes before 'leur'.
After a preposition French switches to stressed pronouns: 'avec moi', not 'avec je'. Same with 'toi', 'lui', 'eux': 'je la prends avec moi'.
'À emporter' = to take away, to go. It's the standard phrase for takeaway food: 'le prenons à emporter' = we're getting it to go.
A reflexive verb in a positive command swaps 'te' for 'toi' and attaches it: 'habille-toi' = get dressed. Only positive commands make this switch.
